extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in religion, free expression, and comedy (Patheos / The Freethinker audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A short news/opinion blog post about an incident in which comedians were arrested and audience members assaulted over alleged blasphemy, highlighting legal charges, public reaction, and safety/ethical issues for performers. Useful as source material about the limits and risks comedians face when their material touches religion or politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPC Section 295-A (deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The five have been booked under Indian Penal Code’s Sections 295-A (deliberate and malicious acts intended to outrage religious feelings)...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is cited as a basis for arrest in cases where performance material is alleged to insult deities or religious beliefs; comedians whose jokes are interpreted as deliberate and malicious toward religion can face criminal charges and arrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPC Section 298 (deliberate intent to wound religious feelings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The five have been booked under Indian Penal Code’s Sections ... section 298 (deliberate intent to wound religious feelings)...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to 295-A but focused on intent to wound religious feelings; performers should be aware that perceived intent, not just content, can trigger legal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPC Section 269 (negligent act likely to spread disease)
rubrics_metrics.description: The five have been booked under Indian Penal Code’s Sections ... section 269 (negligent act likely to spread disease)...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During the COVID-19 pandemic, failure to follow public-health rules at events can be charged as a criminal offence; comedians and event organizers must comply with pandemic-related regulations to avoid legal consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPC Section 188 (disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant)
rubrics_metrics.description: The five have been booked under Indian Penal Code’s Sections ... section 188 (disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant)...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-compliance with lawful orders (for example, public-health or crowd-control directives) can be charged; performers and venues should follow orders from authorities to reduce arrest risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPC Section 34 (common intention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The five have been booked under Indian Penal Code’s Sections ... and section 34 (common intention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When actions are alleged to be carried out with common intention by multiple people (e.g., a group acting together to offend or disobey), participants can be charged jointly; organizers should be mindful that group dynamics can increase legal exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Even art has its limitations." (normative constraint cited by complainant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted in the piece: 'Even art has its limitations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by a complainant to justify stopping the show; indicates a commonly invoked normative boundary — performers operating in communities where audiences hold strong religious/cultural norms should consider that some will view certain jokes as unacceptable and may attempt to stop or punish the performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of mob or vigilante violence when religious sentiments are perceived to be offended
rubrics_metrics.description: They stand accused of ‘outraging religious feelings’ ... some members of the audience at a show ... were attacked and beaten by a gang of Hindu fanatics led by Eklavya Singh Gaur...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that alleged offending material led to a physical assault on audience and performers; beyond legal risk, material that provokes strong religious reaction can create immediate personal-safety hazards for comedians and attendees, so venue security, local context, and potential flashpoints should be assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific targets (deities, cultural symbols, politicians) increase backlash risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Gaur complained ... that the comedians had insulted Hindu deities during the show and also cracked jokes about Home Minister Amit Shah. 'There were jokes on Ganesh and Karthik, a mockery of Indian culture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes directed at revered religious figures, cultural symbols, or powerful politicians are more likely to provoke complaints, legal action, or violent responses; comedians should weigh the comedic value against the heightened risk in a given context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics used by complainants: attending/buying tickets to disrupt and recording the show
rubrics_metrics.description: Gaur said that when he got to know that Munawar is holding a show in Indore, he and his associates bought tickets and went to the event as members of the audience. 'We shot a video and stopped the show by taking the audience out of the cafe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers and performers should be aware that opponents may infiltrate audiences, record performances, and use recordings or claims to file complaints; event admission and security policies can mitigate such tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of evidence and investigation (seizure of digital media, conflicting eyewitness accounts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Town inspector ... said: 'There’s no evidence against him for insulting Hindu deities or Union Minister Amit Shah.' Sharma added: 'We have seized pen drives and hard drives and we are looking into the matter.' Eyewitnesses insist that no religious jokes were cracked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disputes about what was said often hinge on recordings, seized media, and eyewitness testimony; performers and venues should understand that digital evidence can be decisive in investigations and legal proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public support and social-media advocacy can shape narrative and pressure authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Meanwhile, support has been pouring in for Faruqui on social media, with several comics and celebrities voicing support for the performer. Varun Grover shared: 'A fellow Indian, a fellow comedian is in jail ... our systems now just want to brutally silence every voice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid public backing from peers and celebrities can raise awareness, influence public opinion, and apply pressure on authorities; comedians and supporters can use social platforms to mobilize support when legal or physical reprisals occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal process consequences: custody, bail, and detention timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: They were denied bail yesterday ... They are being held in custody until January 13.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegations under these statutes can lead to immediate detention and denial of bail; comedians and organizers should be aware that being charged may result in short-term judicial custody and legal costs even before any substantive determination of guilt.
